title: Uddalaka and Shvetaketu: "you've studied twelve years — do you know That?" (6.1)
hook: a son comes home after twelve years of study, proud and stiff, and his father asks him one question he can't answer
tomorrow: the clay, the gold, the iron

segments.voice: Yesterday: pancagni, the king's five fires, and your line, rain to food to seed to person.
screen: `PANCAGNI — RAIN TO FOOD TO SEED TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: The front door opens. A young man comes home after twelve years away. He's twenty-four. He has memorized the Vedas. He walks in, the text says, swollen with pride, thinking himself very learned, a little stiff with it. Maybe you've met him. Maybe you've been him, home from the first year of college, correcting everyone at dinner. His father watches him for a while. Then he asks one question, and it isn't a test of memory. So begins the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the most studied in Hindu philosophy: a father, a son, and two weeks of lessons.
screen: `HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS.` → `SWOLLEN WITH PRIDE.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The father is Uddalaka Aruni, one of the great teachers of the Upanishads. The son is Shvetaketu, the same young man the king embarrassed yesterday. When Shvetaketu was twelve, his father sent him off to study with a warning: in our family, nobody is a brahmin just by birth. Go and learn. Now he's back, proud of all he knows. And his father asks: since you think so much of yourself, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. How could there be such a teaching, sir? The question isn't asking for one more fact; twelve years of facts are already in his head. It asks whether there's one thing that, once known, makes everything else make sense. A key, not another room. The Upanishads often just call what that key opens That. And the father is gentle. He doesn't mock. He uses a word he'll repeat through all the lessons ahead: somya, my dear, the way you'd talk to someone you love. Then he begins to teach with things from the kitchen and the garden: clay, salt, honey, a seed. Nine times, he'll close a lesson with the same three words.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS EARLIER, A WARNING.` · `THE UNHEARD BECOMES HEARD.` · `A KEY, NOT ANOTHER ROOM.` · `SOMYA, MY DEAR.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING WORTH KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Let what you know come up, your job, your skills, your opinions, what you studied, and set each one down beside you like books on a table; you can pick them all up later. For now, sit with empty hands, and let the father's question hang in the air, unanswered.
Somya, gentle, dear. Uddalaka's word for his son, repeated through the lessons, as he asks whether anyone taught him the one teaching by which the unknown becomes known.
Your line: the one thing worth knowing. Tomorrow, his first lesson: a lump of clay. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.

screen: `DAY 339 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CLAY, THE GOLD, THE IRON.`
